## TL;DR

Tailnet discovery was using Tailscale's display `HostName` as both the SSH
target and the de-duplication key. That collapsed distinct machines that share a
display name (two `omarchy` peers) and turned a Mac mini's spaced/punctuated
display name into an invalid SSH destination. Discovery now derives a stable
MagicDNS label from `DNSName` for SSH and de-duplication, keeps `HostName` as a
separate readable `displayName`, and skips Android/iOS peers that cannot host a
RepoOS server. The existing configured-host fallback, SSH argv shape, JSON
shape and HTTPS URL mapping are preserved. Deterministic fakes cover duplicate
hostnames, punctuation/spaces, MagicDNS names and mobile peers. The Hub's auth
refusal message and the Android Hub / CLI docs now explain the signed-in
requirement and the supported path to discovery.

## Work and rationale

The change is concentrated in `src/core/tailnet-servers.ts`, which is shared by
`repoos servers --tailscale` and `GET /api/servers/tailnet` (the mobile Hub's
server-assisted discovery). The previous `peerFromStatus` did:

- `dnsName = DNSName` minus the trailing dot,
- `host = (HostName ?? DNSName).split(".")[0]`.

That made `HostName` authoritative. Tailscale can report a human-friendly
`HostName` with spaces or punctuation, and two different peers can legitimately
share one. The peer loop then de-duplicated on that `host`, so `bee` and
`thinkpad` disappeared into a single `omarchy` row and the Mac mini was probed as
`Peck’s Mac mini`.

The new parser normalizes `DNSName` through a DNS-label validator, takes its
first label as `host`, and only falls back to `HostName` when it is itself a
valid DNS name. A peer with neither a valid MagicDNS name nor a valid fallback is
skipped rather than sent to SSH. The readable `HostName` is retained as
`displayName` when it differs from the MagicDNS label. De-duplication and
self-exclusion use the MagicDNS identity (`DNSName`, else `host`), so two peers
with the same display name remain distinct while a genuine duplicate entry
collapses.

`collectTailnetServers` now carries `displayName` onto both successful and
unreachable rows, and looks up a configured per-host row by either the MagicDNS
label or the full MagicDNS name. The SSH destination remains the short
MagicDNS label, and host/user still travel as separate SSH argv, so display
names can never become shell syntax or an SSH destination. `tailnetServerUrl`
still prefers the full `dnsName` for URLs, so HTTPS serve mappings and the plain
HTTP fallback keep working.

Mobile peers are filtered during parsing using Tailscale's `OS` field
(`android`, `ios`, `ipados`, `tvos`, `watchos`). Phones and tablets do not run
RepoOS servers and do not accept SSH, so probing them only produced a
misleading "unreachable" row. Explicitly configured hosts are not filtered:
a user who deliberately names a host still gets the real SSH error, which keeps
genuine unreachable server-capable hosts diagnosable.

On the mobile side, `TailnetServer` gained an optional `displayName`, and the
Hub's name fallback now uses it before `host:port`. The auth-refusal copy was
corrected: opening a server in Hub does not transfer the native shell's isolated
WebView session, so the message now points at the web Hub from the same origin
or manual add. Existing HTTPS-only selection and de-duplication by origin are
unchanged.

## Approaches tried

I first considered making `host` the full `DNSName` (for example
`bee.tailc0c173.ts.net`). That would be unambiguous for SSH, but it changes the
existing JSON contract more than necessary and makes the CLI table noisy. The
short MagicDNS label is what the report and existing code call the peer name, and
MagicDNS resolves it on the tailnet. I kept the short label as `host` and used
the full name only where it already mattered: the URL builder and configured-host
lookup.

I also considered marking mobile peers with an `unsupported` row instead of
dropping them. That would expose the device but still avoid an SSH attempt.
However, Hub's row model has no "unsupported" affordance and would render the
row as an addable/unreachable server, which is the misleading outcome the task
asks to remove. Dropping them at parse time is simpler and matches "cannot run a
RepoOS server".

For de-duplication I kept the identity key rather than the `Peer` object key.
Tailscale's object keys are unique node keys, but they are not exposed in the
row model; using `DNSName` keeps the behavior explainable and matches the
acceptance criterion. A peer without a valid MagicDNS identity is skipped rather
than risking a wrong SSH target.

## Challenges and blockers

The main subtlety was preserving compatibility while changing identity. Several
existing tests construct peers with only `HostName`, so the fallback path had to
stay valid. The parser therefore accepts a `HostName` only when it is DNS-safe;
`bee` and `thinkpad` continue to work, while `Peck’s Mac mini` and
`Nothing Phone (3a)` do not. Another subtlety was self-exclusion: comparing
`host` would have excluded a `bee` peer whose display name happened to match the
local machine's display name, so self and peers are compared by MagicDNS
identity instead.

The Hub's signed-in requirement is a real integration limit, not something this
task can remove: the native shell's InAppBrowser cookies are isolated from the
shell's fetch, so an auth-enabled server can still refuse discovery. I did not
try to bypass auth or invent a session. The failure is now plain and actionable,
and the docs say the web build from the same origin (or an auth-disabled server)
is the path that works today. A per-server native session remains the separate
follow-up already recorded as #0304.

No live tailnet or device evidence is claimed here. The regression coverage uses
fake `tailscale status --json` payloads and fake SSH exec functions; the real
hosts were not modified.

## Key learnings

- A display name is not an identity. Tailscale's `DNSName` is the stable,
  DNS-safe key; `HostName` is presentation.
- Filtering at the parser, not at the SSH call, is what prevents a misleading
  failure from ever reaching the UI.
- Optional fields are the safe way to extend discovery JSON: `host` keeps its
  meaning, `displayName` is additive, and older consumers ignore it.
- The Hub's auth story has two separate sessions (shell vs. isolated WebView).
  Documentation and error copy must say that explicitly, or users will retry a
  flow that cannot work from the native shell.
